metadata.title: When Should You Update the Handbook?
metadata.purpose: Answer what actually triggers the need to update an employee handbook -- a date on the calendar, or a change in the law. Lands the carry-out that updates should be tracked by the law that triggers them, not a scheduled review.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible handbook-maintenance account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks when to update the employee handbook. The reflex is to name a date — quarterly, yearly, whenever the calendar says. That reflex is optimizing for scheduling, not for correctness. Liam, in for Bear, on what actually triggers an update.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What updates the handbook -- the calendar?', hesitates on 'calendar', corrects to 'law', lands the real question

props.text:
What updates
the handbook —
the calendar?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('calendar' -> 'law') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a yearly review actually optimizes for: predictable calendar overhead. One afternoon in December, one block on the schedule, done. What it sacrifices is the thing you thought you were buying — a handbook that matches the law. A statute takes effect in March; it does not wait for December. From that day forward the affected section is wrong, and stays wrong for however many months are left until the scheduled read-through. Tidy scheduling, at the cost of accuracy.

shot.new_visual_element: A calendar with one marked review day in December; a law-change icon lighting up in March, far from the marked day, with the handbook page beside it flipping to a struck-through 'current'

production_viz.label: The calendar review, and the gap it leaves
production_viz.mechanic: A year-strip calendar with one day in December ringed and labelled 'REVIEW'. A law-change glyph lights up in March, far from the ringed day. Beside it, a handbook page reading 'current' flips to a struck-through 'current' the instant the glyph lights, while the ringed December day stays untouched and far away.

beats.narration_text: The fix isn't reviewing more often — that just pours effort into the wrong axis. The fix is switching what triggers the work in the first place. Track updates by the specific legal change that forces them, not by a date on the calendar. Watch the anchor: a state raises its paid-leave minimum in the spring. That one change touches exactly one section — the leave policy — not the whole handbook. Trigger-based work is scoped to what actually changed.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a single law-change event connecting by a line to one highlighted handbook section, the rest of the handbook dimmed

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one law change, one section
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A law-change card reading 'paid-leave minimum raised' appears at left. A thin line draws from it to a single highlighted row in a stacked list of handbook sections labelled 'LEAVE POLICY'; every other section in the stack stays dim and untouched. THIS EXACT SECTION ROW RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That section gets a specific fix — new language for the new minimum — logged with what changed, why, and the effective date. That log is doing real work: it replaces a silent overwrite with a record you can audit later. But the design has two failure modes worth naming. A flagged section isn't a finished one — the drafted language still needs a legal read before it ships. And a quiet quarter with no flags doesn't mean the handbook is complete. It means no tracked law changed. Those are not the same claim.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the leave section fills with a dated amendment entry, then splits into 'flagged is not final' and 'quiet is not complete'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- logged, not finished
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 LEAVE POLICY ROW RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in with an amendment entry (what changed / why / effective date) one line at a time, then slides into a small dated log. It splits into two cards: left reads 'section: flagged' with a struck-through 'DONE' beneath it labelled 'flagged is not final'; right reads 'quarter: no flags' with a faint new law-change card appearing at its edge labelled 'quiet is not complete'.

beats.narration_text: A handbook doesn't go out of date on a birthday — it goes out of date the day a law changes. Track updates by the law that triggers them, not a date on the calendar.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — read it with me. Pick one policy in your employee handbook — leave, overtime, remote work, anything. Write down the date it was last actually changed, then find out whether any law touching that topic has changed since. If you can't answer either question, you've just measured the gap this habit exists to close. Go deeper: which policy in your handbook is highest-risk if it's silently stale, and what would it take to move that one policy off the calendar-review track and onto a triggered-update track first? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to audit whether one policy in my employee handbook is silently out of date. Pick one policy — leave, overtime, or remote work — and walk me through it: (1) how would I find the date the policy was last substantively changed, not just re-formatted; (2) what statutes, regulations, or agency guidance in my jurisdiction most commonly touch that policy area; (3) how would I check whether any of those have changed since that date; and (4) if I can't answer (1) or (3), what does that gap tell me about how the handbook is being maintained, and what would a triggered-update process for that one policy actually look like?
